topic: How Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) Store Facts in Transformers

outline.topic: How Multilayer Perceptrons (MLP) Store Facts in Transformers

sections.title: The Analogy: Library vs. Book Content
sections.content: Define the Transformer architecture's duality: Attention mechanisms represent 'retrieval' (pointing to information), while the MLP layers represent 'knowledge storage' (the content itself).
sections.example: Imagine a library. Attention is the 'Index/Catalog' that helps you find the right shelf, while the MLP is the 'Book' where the actual facts are written on the pages.

sections.title: The MLP Mechanism: Key-Value Memories
sections.content: Introduce the MLP as a series of weight matrices. We visualize this as a 'Key-Value' lookup table. The first linear layer acts as a 'Key' detector (pattern matching), and the second acts as a 'Value' generator (outputting the fact).
sections.example: When the model sees 'Paris', the neurons act like a lock. If the input matches the 'City' key, the neurons fire, outputting the stored value 'France'.

sections.title: Visualizing Weights as Knowledge
sections.content: Explain how facts are 'distributed' across neurons. Use a graphical concept: instead of one neuron = one fact, represent it as a 'constellation' of weights. Activation is like a spotlight hitting a specific pattern of neurons.
sections.example: Visual representation of a neural network layer where activating a specific subset of nodes lights up the path representing 'The capital of France is Paris'.

sections.title: The Memory Retrieval Process
sections.content: Summarize the feed-forward cycle: Input vector -> Activation of 'Fact Neurons' -> Projection into output space. Connect this to the concept of 'Model Editing' (how researchers can change facts by altering weights).
sections.example: If a robot mistakenly thinks 'The capital of Japan is Tokyo', we can surgically modify the weights in the MLP layer to 'overwrite' the specific fact-node, changing its output to a new correction.

sections.title: Conclusion and Limitations
sections.content: Conclude by emphasizing that MLPs function as a 'compressed database'. Note that this storage is fuzzy and associative rather than a rigid database.
sections.example: A 'Cloud' of connected dots representing knowledge; it's robust and associative—knowing 'France' is in Europe helps the model infer other facts linked through the same weighted paths.

lecture_lines: Attention mechanisms act like a library's index catalog.
MLP layers store the actual knowledge contents.
Like books, MLPs hold the facts within.

storyboard.title: The MLP Mechanism: Key-Value Memories
lecture_lines: Input vector activates a specific key.
Neurons act like locks for specific patterns.
animations: Display MLP layers as a sequence of rectangles in light blue (#ADD8E6).
Highlight individual weights as small nodes within layers using green (#00FF00).
Animate signal flowing through nodes as arrows in white (#FFFFFF).

storyboard.title: Visualizing Weights as Knowledge
lecture_lines: Facts aren't single nodes, but constellations.
Activation lights up a specific neural path.
This forms the knowledge representation pattern.
Spotlight effect shows fact distribution clearly.
Connections define the stored relational truth.
animations: Visualize a single weight vector in light cyan (#E0FFFF) pointing to an output.
Flash the vector with gold (#FFD700) to represent 'active' knowledge extraction.
Label the vector 'Learned Knowledge' in white (#FFFFFF) above it.

storyboard.title: Conclusion and Limitations
lecture_lines: MLPs function as compressed, fuzzy databases.
